title: How a request flows through the Koa onion
subtitle: One HTTP request through compose, context, request and response
throughline: One incoming HTTP request, from the node server callback down through the middleware onion and back out as a finished response.

chapters.title: From socket to callback
chapters.blurb: An incoming HTTP request enters Koa through app.callback and gets its own per-request context.

story.title: From socket to callback
story.subtitle: One HTTP request through compose, context, request and response

steps.title: From socket to callback
steps.narration: A request arrives at the node server and Koa's `app.callback()` takes over.
steps.say: Every Koa application begins the same way, with one request arriving at a plain node server.

steps.title: A request arrives
steps.narration: A client sends an HTTP request to a **node http server** created by `app.listen()`, which wraps `http.createServer`.
steps.say: It starts when a client sends an HTTP request to a plain node server. Koa does not replace that server. When you call listen, Koa simply hands node a function to run for every request.

steps.title: app.callback hands off
steps.narration: That function is `app.callback()`, which returns the `handleRequest` handler node invokes for each connection.
steps.say: The function node runs is the one returned by app dot callback. For every request, node calls into Koa's handle request, which is the single doorway into the framework.

steps.title: A context is born
steps.narration: First, `createContext(req, res)` builds a fresh `ctx` for this request, wrapping node's raw `req` and `res`.
steps.say: Before any of your code runs, Koa builds a fresh context for this one request. The context wraps the raw node request and response, and it is the single object your middleware will receive.

steps.title: Into the stack
steps.narration: With `ctx` ready, `handleRequest` hands it to the composed **middleware stack** registered with `app.use()`.
steps.say: With the context ready, Koa hands it to the middleware stack. Every function you registered with app dot use is waiting here, in the order you added them.

steps.title: The entry path
steps.narration: The full entry: client to **node server** to `app.callback`, which builds `ctx` and runs your middleware.
steps.say: So the entry path is simple. A request reaches the node server, the callback builds one context, and that context is carried into your middleware. From here, the real journey begins.

chapters.title: The middleware onion
chapters.blurb: compose chains the middleware so control flows downstream through next, then unwinds back upstream.

story.title: The middleware onion
story.subtitle: One HTTP request through compose, context, request and response

steps.title: The middleware onion
steps.narration: `compose` chains your middleware into the famous onion, where control flows down through `next()` and unwinds back up.
steps.say: Koa's signature is the onion. Control flows down through your middleware, then unwinds and flows back up. Let's see how that shape is built.

steps.title: compose chains them
steps.narration: At startup, `compose` from `koa-compose` folds the array of middleware into one function that threads `next` from each onto the following one.
steps.say: At startup, a function called compose folds your whole list of middleware into a single function. It does this by giving each middleware a next that points at the one after it. That chaining is the entire trick behind the onion.

steps.title: Down to the logger
steps.narration: The composed function invokes the first middleware, the **logger**, passing it `ctx` and its `next`.
steps.say: When a request comes in, the composed function calls the first middleware, our logger. It receives the context and a next function, exactly the signature you write by hand.

steps.title: await next goes deeper
steps.narration: The logger runs its capture code, then `await next()` suspends it and passes control to the next middleware, **x-response-time**.
steps.say: The logger does its early work, then awaits next. Awaiting next suspends the logger and passes control downstream to the next middleware, which records a start time. Each await dives one layer deeper.

steps.title: The innermost handler
steps.narration: Control reaches the innermost **responder**, which sets `ctx.body = 'Hello World'`. There is no more downstream, so the stack starts to unwind.
steps.say: Control reaches the innermost middleware, the responder. It sets the body on the context to Hello World. There is nothing further downstream, so this is the center of the onion, and the stack now begins to unwind.

steps.title: Back upstream
steps.narration: As each `await next()` resolves, the middleware resume in reverse. **x-response-time** computes the duration and `ctx.set('X-Response-Time', ...)`.
steps.say: Now the awaits resolve in reverse order. The timing middleware wakes up, measures how long everything below it took, and writes the response time header onto the context. This is the upstream half of the onion.

steps.title: The logger has the last word
steps.narration: Finally the **logger** resumes after its `await next()`, reads `ctx.response.get('X-Response-Time')`, and logs the line.
steps.say: Last to resume is the logger, the first one we entered. It reads the response time header back off the context and prints its log line. First in, last out, just like a stack.

steps.title: Down and back up
steps.narration: The whole cascade: `compose` runs logger, x-response-time, then responder downstream, and they resume in reverse, all sharing one `ctx`.
steps.say: That is the onion in full. Compose sends control down through each middleware, the innermost one sets the body, and then every layer resumes in reverse. One context is shared by all of them the entire time.

chapters.title: Context, request and response
chapters.blurb: ctx delegates to its Koa request and response objects, which wrap node's raw req and res.

story.title: Context, request and response
story.subtitle: One HTTP request through compose, context, request and response

steps.title: Context, request and response
steps.narration: `ctx` delegates to a Koa `request` and `response`, which wrap node's raw `req` and `res`.
steps.say: The context your middleware holds is really three layers in one. Let's pull them apart.

steps.title: ctx is the receiver
steps.narration: Each middleware receives `ctx`, the **Context** from `lib/context.js`. It encapsulates one request and its response into a single object.
steps.say: At the center is ctx, the context. It is created once per request and is the receiver your middleware works with. Koa puts the most common operations right here so you rarely reach for anything lower.

steps.title: ctx delegates
steps.narration: Many accessors on `ctx` simply delegate: `ctx.path` and `ctx.method` go to **ctx.request**; `ctx.body` and `ctx.status` go to **ctx.response**.
steps.say: Most of the context is an illusion. When you read the path or method, the context quietly delegates to the request object. When you set the body or status, it delegates to the response object. Two real objects live just behind it.

steps.title: request wraps node req
steps.narration: The Koa **request** in `lib/request.js` is an abstraction over node's `req`. Getters like `get url()` return `this.req.url`; `header` returns `this.req.headers`.
steps.say: The Koa request is a thin abstraction over node's raw incoming message. Ask it for the url or the headers and it reads them straight off the node request. It adds friendly extras like host, protocol, and the parsed query.

steps.title: response wraps node res
steps.narration: The Koa **response** in `lib/response.js` wraps node's `res`. `get status()` returns `this.res.statusCode`; setting `status` writes back to `this.res.statusCode`.
steps.say: Symmetrically, the Koa response wraps node's server response. Its status getter reads the node status code, and setting the status writes it back. Notice one twist, though.

steps.title: The 404 default
steps.narration: By default `response.status` is `404`, unlike node's `res.statusCode` of `200`. Setting `ctx.body` flips it to `200` unless you set status explicitly.
steps.say: By default the Koa response status is a four oh four, not node's two hundred. That is deliberate. The moment you assign a body, Koa promotes the status to two hundred for you, unless you have already set one explicitly.

steps.title: Three layers, one request
steps.narration: `ctx` delegates to `ctx.request` and `ctx.response`, each wrapping node's `req` and `res`, so your code touches one object instead of two raw ones.
steps.say: So the context is three layers. It delegates to a request and a response, and each of those wraps a raw node object. You write against one friendly surface, and Koa keeps the messy node details just out of sight.

chapters.title: Responding and the full journey
chapters.blurb: After middleware settles, app.respond writes the body to node, and errors route through ctx.onerror.

story.title: Responding and the full journey
story.subtitle: One HTTP request through compose, context, request and response

steps.title: Responding and the full journey
steps.narration: Once the onion settles, `app.respond` reads `ctx.body` and writes the reply; thrown errors detour through `ctx.onerror`.
steps.say: Once the onion has fully unwound, Koa still has to actually send the reply. Let's follow the request all the way out, including what happens when something throws.
steps.coverSubtitle: The onion settles, the reply ships

steps.title: The promise settles
steps.narration: `handleRequest` runs the composed **middleware onion** as a promise. When it resolves, control returns to Koa with `ctx` fully populated.
steps.say: Remember that the whole onion is one promise. The client is still waiting while it runs. When that promise resolves, control comes back to Koa, and the context now holds everything the middleware decided.

steps.title: app.respond takes over
steps.narration: Unless `ctx.respond` is `false`, Koa calls `respond(ctx)`. It inspects `ctx.body` and decides how to finish the node response.
steps.say: Now Koa's respond function takes over. As long as you have not opted out by setting respond to false, it looks at the body you placed on the context and works out exactly how to end the node response.

steps.title: Writing the response
steps.narration: `respond` writes status and headers, then ends node's `res` with the body, a buffer, a string, or a piped stream.
steps.say: Respond sets the final status and headers, then writes the body to node's raw response and ends it. If the body is a stream it gets piped, if it is a string or buffer it is written directly, and a HEAD request gets the headers with no body.

steps.title: The reply ships
steps.narration: Node flushes the finished `res` back over the socket. The client finally receives its status, headers, and body.
steps.say: Node flushes that finished response back across the socket, and the client receives its status, headers, and body at last. The request's journey is complete.

steps.title: When middleware throws
steps.narration: If any middleware throws, the promise rejects and `ctx.onerror(err)` runs: it unsets headers, sets a status, and emits `app.emit('error')`.
steps.say: But what if something throws? Then the promise rejects, and Koa routes the error through the context's onerror handler. It clears any partial headers, picks a sensible status, emits an error event on the app, and still produces a clean response.

steps.title: The whole journey
steps.narration: End to end: client to **onion** to `ctx`, then `app.respond` writes node's `res` back to the client; a throw detours through `ctx.onerror`.
steps.say: So here is the whole journey. A request enters the onion, the middleware shape the context, respond writes node's response, and the reply travels back to the client. And if anything throws along the way, onerror catches it and still sends a clean answer. That is a request's secret life inside Koa.
